title: Design a Web Crawler
oneLiner: A search engine crawler as a 45-minute design round: the URL frontier, politeness, deduplication and recrawl scheduling.
keyTakeaway: A crawler's raw throughput is modest; what makes it hard is fetching politely from millions of hosts while always working on the most valuable URLs. Split the frontier into priority queues and per-host queues, partition hosts across machines so politeness needs no coordination, and deduplicate both URLs and content so the fetch budget isn't wasted.
explanation:
Same format as the other walk-throughs: write your answer for each stage first, then compare it with the model answer and tick what you covered. The 45-minute flow is the same; what changes is where the difficulty sits.

A crawler has no users waiting on it and sets its own pace, so the usual worries about read latency and traffic peaks mostly disappear. A billion pages a month is only about 400 fetches a second, which a few dozen machines handle. The estimation stage should show that the pressure is elsewhere: around 20,000 extracted links a second that each need a "seen before?" check, a frontier holding ten times more URLs than the monthly budget, and a politeness rule (roughly one request per host every few seconds) that forces the crawler to spread its work across tens of thousands of hosts at once.

The deep dive almost always starts with the URL frontier: how to combine priority with per-host rate limits, which is what Mercator's front and back queues do. From there interviewers move to robots.txt and DNS, URL normalisation and Bloom filters, near-duplicate content with SimHash, deciding when to recrawl a page, and crawler traps. Pick the ones they react to and explain the mechanism, not just the name. Expect follow-ups such as "a site starts returning 503s halfway through: what does your crawler do?" or "one site generates a new URL for every calendar day forever: how do you notice?"
